2:
SAY:
- Read the cultural sensitivity statement aloud, in a calm voice.
- 'In this story we will read about the Coorong and the Ngarrindjeri Country it sits on.'
- 'Some of the language reflects the time it was written, not how we speak today.'

DO:
- Pause briefly so students take it in.
- Move on without inviting discussion.

TEACHER NOTES:
Deliver as a one-minute orientation at the start of every lesson in the unit. Not a discussion task.

SENSITIVITY ADVISORY:
- What it is: references to deceased persons, historical perspectives, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures.
- Framing language: see SAY.
- Watch for: students who may have personal or cultural connections; signs of discomfort during reading.
- Protocol: pause if a student is distressed, offer a quiet seat or water, let the student step out and rejoin without comment.

WATCH FOR:
- Body language at the moment of reading; respond quietly without making the student the focus.

[Stage: Lesson Orientation]
7:
SAY:
- 'Today we are reading more of Storm Boy, learning three new words, and learning to combine sentences using FANBOYS conjunctions.'
- Read each Success Criterion aloud and point as you go.
- 'If joining sentences feels new, that is okay. We will build it together.'

DO:
- Point to each SC.
- Tap the FANBOYS criterion twice so students hold it as today's writing focus.

TEACHER NOTES:
The FANBOYS criterion is what the booklet task assesses. Comprehension and vocab feed into the writing.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who cannot say the FANBOYS goal back in their own words; flag for extra modelling later.

[Stage: LI and SC]
8:
SAY:
- 'On your desk: pencil, booklet and novel, mini whiteboard and texta.'
- 'Thumbs up when you are ready.'

DO:
- Scan for thumbs.
- Hand spare whiteboards or textas to anyone missing one.

TEACHER NOTES:
Ready-to-learn check. Multiple whiteboard responses follow, so do not skip.

WATCH FOR:
- Students still searching trays; pre-place spares on a side table.

[Stage: Materials]

SOURCES:

SAY:
- 'We are about to read part of Storm Boy together. Listening and following along is the first job.'

DO:
- Settle the class with novels open.
- Ready your bookmarks and pause-point markers.

TEACHER NOTES:
Reading mode (read-aloud, partner, choral) is teacher choice. Decide before the lesson.

WATCH FOR:

[Stage: Text-Level Reading]
10:
SAY:
- 'We are reading pages 57 to 62 of Storm Boy now.'
- 'I will pause when we hit a word or moment we need to think about.'
- 'If you hear a word you do not know, mark it with your finger.'

DO:
- Pre-mark your novel with pause points and queries before the lesson.
- Read at a steady pace; pause where marked, ask a planned query, take 2 to 3 responses, keep reading.
- Note any vocabulary students flag.

TEACHER NOTES:
No handbook supplied to this notes pass. Confirm pause points and any literary devices using your Literature Study Guide before teaching.

WATCH FOR:
- Students losing the page; quietly point without breaking flow.
- Comprehension stumbles at multi-clause sentences; that is exactly today's writing focus.

[Stage: Read-Aloud]
11:
SAY:
- 'Three new words from this part of the story. Listen for each word, then we will use it.'

DO:
- Display the slide and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. Today's target words are wounded, seized and coiled.

[Stage: Vocabulary]
12:
SOURCES:
- Macquarie Dictionary, 2024.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'The word is wounded. Say it with me. Wounded.'
- 'Wounded means hurt or injured. It is an adjective, so it describes a person, animal or thing.'
- 'In Storm Boy, the tugboat looked like a wounded whale when the waves crashed over it.'
- Ask: 'Say wounded with me.' Expected: 'Wounded.'

DO:
- Point to the picture as you say the meaning.
- Run the affixes line: 'wound, wounds, wounding, wounded'.
- Point to the word associations: hurt, injured, damaged.

TEACHER NOTES:
Keep the focus on the adjective use. The boat is being described like an injured animal.

MISCONCEPTIONS:
- Misconception: wounded and wound mean the same thing.
  Why: shared spelling root.
  Impact: students misuse wounded as a verb of action.
  Quick correction: 'Wounded describes how someone is. A wound is the actual injury.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing wounded with wound; address only if it surfaces.

[Stage: I Do | Vocabulary]
13:
SAY:
- 'Look at the four emojis. Which one fits with wounded?'
- Ask: 'Show me your number on your fingers - one, two, three or four. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan finger responses.
- Cold call two students for their reasoning.

TEACHER NOTES:
Reasoning is the marker, not the chosen emoji. Look for justification using 'hurt or injured'.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick a sad face vs hurt face; both are defensible if they explain.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
14:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. If he was wounded he would or wouldn't need medical attention.'
- 'On your whiteboards write would or wouldn't, then your reason. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Pick one student to read theirs aloud with the reason.

TEACHER NOTES:
Either answer is acceptable if the reason uses 'hurt or injured'.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who write the answer with no reason; prompt 'because...'.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
15:
SAY:
- 'Read with me. Our soccer team would or wouldn't win if our star player was wounded.'
- 'Whiteboards: would or wouldn't, plus the reason. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Take 2 to 3 reasons.

WATCH FOR:
- Guesses without reasoning; redirect to 'hurt or injured'.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
16:
SAY:
- 'Last sentence. The dog would or wouldn't be wounded if his owner kept it on a leash during the walk.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Pick one student to defend each option.

WATCH FOR:
- Mixed answers are fine; reasoning is the test.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
17:
SAY:
- 'I will read each statement. You decide if it makes sense for someone who is wounded.'
- Ask each statement; expected: students respond with full sentences using 'because'.

DO:
- Give think time after each statement.
- Cold call non-volunteers and insist on full sentences.

TEACHER NOTES:
Full-sentence responses build oral language. Yes or no answers are not enough here.

WATCH FOR:
- Short yes/no answers; redirect to 'because...'.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
18:
SAY:
- 'Three of these words are similar to wounded. One is unlike wounded.'
- Ask: 'Show me your fingers - one for sore, two for tired, three for injured, four for hurting. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 2 (tired).

DO:
- Scan responses.
- Take one student's reasoning before revealing.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers 1-4
Script:
- 'Show me which word does not fit with wounded. Three, two, one.'
- Scan for: a clear majority on 2 (tired).
PROCEED:
- Confirm tired and remind class that sore, injured and hurting all describe being hurt.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students confuse tired (low energy) with hurting (in pain).
- Reteach with a quick example: 'After running, I am tired. After falling, I am hurting - my body has been wounded.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again - which is unlike wounded?'

TEACHER NOTES:
Word-association is the threshold check before the build-a-sentence task.

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing sore as the odd one out; address that sore still belongs to the hurt family.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
19:
SAY:
- 'Build a sentence using wounded. The blank was wounded because blank.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'
- 'Swap with your partner when I tap the bell. Read theirs.'

DO:
- Circulate and read 5 boards.
- Reveal the sample: 'The pelican was wounded because hunters sneaked into the sanctuary.'
- Cold call 2 students to read theirs.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show
Script:
- 'Hold your board up. I am looking for wounded used correctly with a reason.'
- Scan for: 80% complete sentences with wounded as an adjective.
PROCEED:
- Move to seized.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students use wounded as a verb of action.
- Reteach with the underline test: 'The dog was wounded - was wounded describes the state, not the action.'
- Re-check: 'Rewrite so wounded describes who or what.'

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the active-practice exit for wounded. Spelling is a quick fix on boards.

WATCH FOR:
- Spelling errors on wounded.
- Students using wounded as the verb only.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
20:
SOURCES:
- Macquarie Dictionary, 2024.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'The word is seized. Say it with me. Seized.'
- 'If you seize something, you take hold of it quickly and firmly. It is a verb - it tells us about an action.'
- 'In Storm Boy, the captain seized the fishing line and fastened it to the end of the rope.'
- Ask: 'Say seized with me.' Expected: 'Seized.'

DO:
- Point to the picture as you say the meaning.
- Run the affixes line: 'seize, seizes, seized, seizing'.
- Point to the word associations: grab, take hold, grasp.

TEACHER NOTES:
Seized is fast AND firm. Both qualities matter when judging student examples.

WATCH FOR:
- Students saying 'see-zd' incorrectly; model the long ee sound and the d ending.

[Stage: I Do | Vocabulary]
21:
SAY:
- 'Look at the picture. Is something being seized?'
- 'Whiteboards: seized or not seized. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Seized.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student why; look for 'taking hold quickly and firmly'.

WATCH FOR:
- Students with weak reasoning; redirect to the two qualities.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
22:
SAY:
- 'New picture. Whiteboards: seized or not seized. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Not seized.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student why; look for slow, gentle, or different from grabbing.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
23:
SAY:
- 'Last image. Whiteboards: seized or not seized. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Seized.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Acknowledge any student who got all three correct.

WATCH FOR:
- Students calling everything seized; remind them seized needs both quick and firm.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
24:
SAY:
- 'Six words. Which ones are associated with seized?'
- 'Tell your partner your two best matches.'
- Ask: 'Why did you pick those?' Expected: language tied to firm and quick.

DO:
- Time partner talk for 60 seconds.
- Cold call 3 students.
- Confirm: firmly, grasped, quickly, grabbed. Softly and dropped do not fit.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Cold Call after Wait Time
Script:
- 'Tell me one word associated with seized and why.'
- Scan for: students naming firmly, grasped, quickly or grabbed with a 'because' reason.
PROCEED:
- Move on.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students pick softly because they are matching to a hand image, not the meaning.
- Reteach by acting: grab firmly vs touch softly. 'Seized is fast and strong.'
- Re-check: 'Show me your two best words for seized.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick dropped; that is the opposite.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
25:
SAY:
- 'Read the sentence: The seagull quickly grabbed the chip from my hand.'
- 'Rephrase using seized. Whiteboards. One minute.'
- 'Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Reveal: 'The seagull seized the chip from my hand.'
- Ask one student to read theirs.

TEACHER NOTES:
Seized already implies quick - keeping or dropping 'quickly' both work.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who lose other parts of the sentence; only the verb changes.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
26:
SAY:
- 'Read the sentence: The cat caught the mouse with its paws.'
- 'Rephrase using seized. Whiteboards. One minute.'
- 'Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Reveal: 'The cat seized the mouse with its paws.'
- Take one student response.

WATCH FOR:
- Students replacing the wrong word; only caught becomes seized.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
27:
SAY:
- 'Two scenarios. Which uses seized correctly?'
- 'A: The man seized the rope to stop himself from falling.'
- 'B: The child seized the egg from the carton to make sure it didn't crack.'
- Ask: 'A or B on your fingers. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: A.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student to defend A; look for 'quickly and firmly'.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers A or B
Script:
- 'A or B for seized. Show me.'
- Scan for: clear majority on A.
PROCEED:
- Confirm A and explain B is too gentle.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: any quick action is seized.
- Reteach by example: 'You would not seize an egg or a kitten - those need gentle hands.'
- Re-check: 'Choose again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students reading only one scenario before choosing.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
28:
SAY:
- 'A or B for seized.'
- 'A: The teacher seized the child's sore arm to check it wasn't broken.'
- 'B: The firefighter seized the hose and rushed towards the burning building.'
- Ask: 'Three, two, one, show.' Expected: B.

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student to defend B.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Show Fingers A or B
Script:
- 'A or B for seized. Show me.'
- Scan for: clear majority on B.
PROCEED:
- Confirm B and explain A is too rough for a sore arm.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students miss that seized is too forceful for a sore arm.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Match the verb to the situation. Firefighters need force; sore arms need care.'
- Re-check: 'Show me again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who defend A by saying the teacher is helping; redirect to the strength of seized.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
29:
SAY:
- 'Look at the picture. Write a sentence about it using seized.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'
- 'When I click, an example appears. Yours can be different.'

DO:
- Circulate and read 5 boards.
- Reveal the model and read it aloud.
- Cold call one student to share.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show
Script:
- 'Hold up your sentence. I am looking for seized used as a verb meaning grabbed quickly and firmly.'
- Scan for: 80% use seized correctly with detail.
PROCEED:
- Move to coiled.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students write seized with no reason or detail.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Strong sentences with seized tell us who, what, and why or how.'
- Re-check: 'Add a because clause and show again.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students using seized to mean noticed or saw.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
30:
SOURCES:
- Macquarie Dictionary, 2024.

SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'The word is coiled. Say it with me. Coiled.'
- 'If something is coiled, it is wound around in rings, usually one on top of or beside the other. It is a verb.'
- 'In Storm Boy, the man tied pieces of fishing line together and coiled them on the sand.'
- Ask: 'Say coiled with me.' Expected: 'Coiled.'

DO:
- Use your hand to draw a coiling spiral in the air.
- Run affixes: 'coil, coils, coiling, coiled'.
- Point to associations: curl, spiral, wind, curve, loop.

TEACHER NOTES:
Coiled means rings stacked, not just rolled forward.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing coiled with rolled; clarify rings vs forward roll.

[Stage: I Do | Vocabulary]
31:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards: coiled or not coiled. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Not coiled.'

DO:
- Scan.
- Ask one student why; look for 'no rings' or 'just straight'.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
32:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards: coiled or not coiled. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Coiled.'

DO:
- Scan.
- Ask one student to point out the rings.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
33:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards: coiled or not coiled. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Coiled.'

DO:
- Scan.
- Take one quick reason.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
34:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards: coiled or not coiled. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Not coiled.'

DO:
- Scan boards.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
35:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards: coiled or not coiled. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Not coiled.'

DO:
- Scan boards.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
36:
SAY:
- 'Last image. Whiteboards: coiled or not coiled. Three, two, one, show.' Expected: 'Coiled.'

DO:
- Scan.
- Acknowledge whole-class accuracy if most got the set right.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who flip every slide; check they are looking for rings, not curves.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
37:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards. Draw a line down the middle.'
- 'On one side, words similar to coiled. On the other, words different from coiled.'
- 'Words to sort: spiral, straight, pointed, curved.'
- 'Three minutes. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Confirm: similar - spiral and curved. Different - straight and pointed.
- Ask one student to defend each side.

WATCH FOR:
- Students placing pointed as similar; clarify pointed is sharp, not curved.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
38:
SAY:
- 'Talk to your partner. How are these two words connected? Coiled and spiral.'
- 'One minute.'
- Ask 3 pairs to share.

DO:
- Time partner talk.
- Cold call three pairs.
- Reveal: coiled means wound around in rings; spiral is the shape coiled things take.

TEACHER NOTES:
Word associations are linked, not synonyms. Make that explicit.

WATCH FOR:
- Students saying 'they mean the same thing'; clarify connected vs identical.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
39:
SAY:
- 'Three sentences. One uses coiled incorrectly. Read with me.'
- 'A: The garden hose was coiled to prevent it from getting kinked.'
- 'B: The boy coiled the ball towards the goal post when he was kicking a goal.'
- 'C: The snake coiled itself around a branch.'
- Ask: 'A, B or C? Show me. Three, two, one.' Expected: B.

DO:
- Scan.
- Ask one student to suggest a better verb for B (kicked, curved).

WATCH FOR:
- Students choosing C because of the snake; remind them snakes literally coil.

[Stage: We Do | Vocabulary]
40:
SAY:
- 'Look at the picture. Write a sentence using coiled. Three minutes.'
- 'When I click, a sample appears. Yours can be different.'

DO:
- Circulate, read 5 boards.
- Reveal sample: 'She coiled the rope neatly before placing it on the deck.'
- Cold call one student.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show
Script:
- 'Hold up your sentence with coiled.'
- Scan for: 80% use coiled to mean wound around in rings.
PROCEED:
- Move to the booklet task.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students use coiled to mean any twisty action.
- Reteach by drawing: 'Coiled has rings stacked - draw a coil in the air with your finger.'
- Re-check: 'Rewrite so it shows the rings.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing 'coiled the snake' instead of 'the snake coiled itself'.

[Stage: CFU | Vocabulary]
41:
SAY:
- 'Open your booklet to Lesson 16 Vocabulary.'
- 'Complete the tasks for wounded, seized and coiled.'
- 'If a word feels new, look back at the slides.'

DO:
- Hand out booklets.
- Set the timer for the booklet block.
- Circulate; read first 2 to 3 answers per student.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: pair with a peer to talk through one example for each word before writing.
- Extra Notes: provide the slide vocabulary card if needed.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: write one sentence that uses two of the three words together.

TEACHER NOTES:
Flag students who cannot use any of the three words; they need extra modelling in the writing segment.

WATCH FOR:
- Students copying example sentences from earlier slides.

[Stage: You Do | Vocabulary]
42:
SAY:
- 'Now we move to writing. The skill today is combining two short sentences into one stronger sentence.'

DO:
- Display the slide and move on.

TEACHER NOTES:
Section divider. Slides 44 to 49 review simple sentences and FANBOYS - skip if your class is confident.

[Stage: Sentence-Level Writing]
43:
TEACHER NOTES:
The slides immediately after this divider are hidden by default. Unhide slides 44 to 47 only if your class needs to revise simple sentences and subject/verb identification.

[Stage: Optional Review]
44:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'A simple sentence has one complete idea, a subject - who or what - and a verb - the doing word. Capital letter at the start, punctuation mark at the end.'
- 'Read with me: The pelican flies.'
- Ask: 'What is the subject?' Expected: 'Pelican.' Ask: 'What is the verb?' Expected: 'Flies.'
- 'If this feels new, that is okay. We will build it together.'

DO:
- Underline subject and verb in your example.
- Point to the capital and the punctuation.

TEACHER NOTES:
Prerequisite slide. Skip if your class confidently identifies subject and verb.

[Stage: I Do | Sentence Review]
45:
SAY:
- 'On your whiteboards write: Mr Percival drops a line across the ship.'
- 'Underline the subject once and the verb twice. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards.
- Ask one student to share. Confirm subject: Mr Percival. Verb: drops.

WATCH FOR:
- Students underlining 'a line' as subject; remind them the subject is who or what is doing.

[Stage: We Do | Sentence Review]
46:
SAY:
- 'New sentence: Hide-Away and Fingerbone shouted together.'
- 'Subject and verb on your boards. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards. Confirm subject: Hide-Away and Fingerbone. Verb: shouted.
- Highlight that two names together can be one subject group.

WATCH FOR:
- Students underlining only one name as subject.

[Stage: We Do | Sentence Review]
47:
SAY:
- 'New sentence: Fingerbone and Hide-Away hauled the end of the big rope.'
- 'Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards. Confirm subject: Fingerbone and Hide-Away. Verb: hauled.

WATCH FOR:
- Students underlining 'rope' as the verb because it is concrete; reinforce verb is the doing word.

[Stage: We Do | Sentence Review]
48:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'A compound sentence is two simple sentences joined together.'
- 'The recipe: independent clause, comma, FANBOYS word, independent clause.'
- 'I need to check that I have two complete sentences before I join them.'
- 'Each side could stand alone.'

DO:
- Read the structure twice, pointing to each part.
- Write a live example: 'The waves were huge, and the boat was sinking.'
- Underline both clauses, circle the comma and the FANBOYS word.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the core teaching point. Keep your live example up for the rest of the lesson.

[Stage: I Do | Compound Sentences]
49:
SAY:
- 'FANBOYS is a memory trick. Each letter stands for a coordinating conjunction.'
- 'F-A-N-B-O-Y-S. For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So.'
- Ask: 'Say it with me.' Expected: 'For, and, nor, but, or, yet, so.'

DO:
- Lead a choral chant of FANBOYS twice.
- Write the seven words vertically on the board.

TEACHER NOTES:
Display the FANBOYS list nearby for the rest of the lesson.

WATCH FOR:
- Students confusing 'for' the conjunction with 'for' the preposition; clarify quickly only if it surfaces.

[Stage: I Do | FANBOYS]
50:
SAY:
- 'Mark up this sentence on your whiteboards.'
- 'We could throw a line in the water, but the boat is too far.'
- 'Underline the two independent clauses. Circle the FANBOYS word and the comma.'
- 'Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards. Confirm clauses, FANBOYS: but, comma before but.
- Cold call one student to walk the class through their marking.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who circle 'but' but miss the comma; the comma before FANBOYS is key.

[Stage: We Do | Compound Sentences]
51:
SAY:
- 'New sentence: Storm Boy was determined to rescue the men, so he devised a plan.'
- 'Mark the clauses, the comma, and the FANBOYS word. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards. FANBOYS: so. Comma before so.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who underline only the verbs; remind them an independent clause has its own subject and verb.

[Stage: We Do | Compound Sentences]
52:
SAY:
- 'Last one: Hide-Away wraps a thin rope line to the lookout post, and they carefully begin the rescue.'
- 'Mark it up. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards. FANBOYS: and.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who think 'they' cannot be a subject; remind them pronouns count.

[Stage: We Do | Compound Sentences]
53:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first.'
- 'Why do we combine sentences? Three reasons: when they are about the same subject, to stop using the same noun over and over, and because longer sentences make our writing more interesting.'

DO:
- Read the three reasons.
- Add a quick example: 'Storm Boy ran. Storm Boy yelled.' becomes 'Storm Boy ran and yelled.'

TEACHER NOTES:
Purpose framing for the I Do that follows. Students often combine without knowing why.

[Stage: I Do | Combining]
54:
SAY:
- 'Three tools: commas, conjunctions, and pronoun references.'
- 'Commas separate. Conjunctions like FANBOYS join. Pronouns - he, she, it, they - replace nouns we have already used.'

DO:
- Write 'Storm Boy was tired. Storm Boy kept going.' on the board.
- Show the change: 'Storm Boy was tired, but he kept going.'
- Highlight comma, but, and pronoun he.

TEACHER NOTES:
Keep your live example up for We Do.

[Stage: I Do | Toolkit]
55:
SAY:
- 'On your whiteboards write the noun and the pronoun reference in this sentence.'
- 'Mr Percival sailed over the pebble, but he changed his mind and landed back on the beach.'
- 'Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan boards. Noun: Mr Percival. Pronoun: he.
- Ask: 'Why did the writer use he instead of repeating Mr Percival?'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show
Script:
- 'Hold up your noun and pronoun.'
- Scan for: 80% have Mr Percival and he.
PROCEED:
- Move to the next We Do.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students choose 'his' instead of 'he'.
- Reteach with the rule: 'His shows belonging - his mind. He stands in for the doer.'
- Re-check: 'Write just the pronoun that replaces Mr Percival.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students circling pebble or beach as nouns; we want the noun the pronoun is replacing.

[Stage: CFU | Pronoun Reference]
56:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards. Why could the people in the damaged tugboat not reach the shore?'
- 'Write two simple sentences. Each needs a subject and a verb. Three minutes.'
- 'Pair-share to check.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal modelled sentences: 'The storm was too wild. The storm made it hard for the men to swim.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing one long sentence with 'and'; bring them back to two simple sentences.

[Stage: We Do | Build Two]
57:
SAY:
- 'Watch this first. I will combine these two sentences.'
- 'Step one: I find the noun that repeats. The storm appears in both.'
- 'Step two: I replace one noun with a pronoun. The storm becomes it.'
- 'Step three: I join with a coordinating conjunction. The storm was too wild, plus so, plus it made it hard for the men to swim.'
- 'Step four: I add a comma before the FANBOYS word.'
- 'Final sentence: The storm was too wild, so it made it hard for the men to swim.'

DO:
- Walk through the four steps slowly, pointing at each.
- Underline the comma and FANBOYS word in the final sentence.

TEACHER NOTES:
This is the model for the four steps. Keep them visible for every We Do that follows.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy without watching the steps; emphasise watching first.

[Stage: I Do | Combining Steps]
58:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards. What happened in the morning?'
- 'Two simple sentences. Three minutes.'
- 'Pair-share to check.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'Storm Boy could see the tugboat. The tugboat was lying like a wounded whale.'
- Note that 'wounded' is one of today's vocab words.

WATCH FOR:
- Students unsure what to write; refer them to the page we read.

[Stage: We Do | Build Two]
59:
SAY:
- 'Combine those two sentences using our four steps.'
- Ask: 'What is the repeated noun?' Expected: 'Tugboat.'
- 'Replace one with a pronoun. Join with a FANBOYS word. Add a comma.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes. Show me your combined sentence.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'Storm Boy could see the tugboat, and it was lying like a wounded whale.'
- Ask one student to read theirs.

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show
Script:
- 'Show me your combined sentence with a comma and a FANBOYS word.'
- Scan for: 80% have a pronoun and a comma before the FANBOYS word.
PROCEED:
- Move to the next pair.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students use 'and' without a comma, OR a comma without a FANBOYS word.
- Reteach with the rule: 'Comma plus FANBOYS, always together.'
- Re-check: 'Show me both - the comma AND the FANBOYS word.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick a FANBOYS word that does not fit the meaning.

[Stage: CFU | Combining]
60:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards. What is Storm Boy's plan?'
- 'Two simple sentences. Pair-share to check.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'Storm Boy devises a plan to rescue the men. Mr Percival has to fly a long fishing line out to the men.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing one long sentence; redirect to two short ideas.

[Stage: We Do | Build Two]
61:
SAY:
- Ask: 'What noun repeats?' Expected: 'The men.'
- 'Replace one with a pronoun. Pick a FANBOYS word. So fits because it shows cause and effect.'
- 'Add a comma. Whiteboards. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'Storm Boy devises a plan to rescue the men, so Mr Percival has to fly a long fishing line out to them.'
- Cold call one student.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using 'and' instead of 'so'; discuss which FANBOYS shows the why.

[Stage: We Do | Combining]
62:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards. What happened the first time Mr Percival was asked to fly out?'
- 'Two simple sentences. Pair-share.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'Hide-Away gave the fishing line and sinker to Mr Percival. Mr Percival didn't understand what to do.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students writing about a different attempt; re-anchor in the first try.

[Stage: We Do | Build Two]
63:
SAY:
- Ask: 'What noun repeats?' Expected: 'Mr Percival.'
- 'Replace with a pronoun. He.'
- 'But fits because there is a contrast - he was given the line, but he didn't understand.'
- 'Add a comma. Whiteboards. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'Hide-Away gave the fishing line and sinker to Mr Percival, but he didn't understand what to do.'
- Read aloud.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using 'so' instead of 'but'; discuss whether contrast or cause fits.

[Stage: We Do | Combining]
64:
SAY:
- 'Whiteboards. Why were Storm Boy, Hide-Away and Fingerbone having trouble rescuing the men?'
- 'Two simple sentences. Pair-share.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'They could see four men clinging to the boat. The boat was too far to throw a line.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who only mention the storm; push for two clear ideas.

[Stage: We Do | Build Two]
65:
SAY:
- 'Combine. This time, do not use and or but. Push yourself to use a different FANBOYS word.'
- Ask: 'What noun repeats?' Expected: 'The boat.'
- 'Replace with a pronoun. It.'
- 'Yet works - it shows surprise and contrast.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'They could see four men clinging to the boat, yet it was too far to throw the line.'
- Cold call one student.

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: allow but or and; flag for return at the extension.
- Extra Notes: focus on the comma plus FANBOYS structure first.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: combine using yet or so and explain why it fits the meaning.
- Extra Notes: justify the FANBOYS choice to a partner.

WATCH FOR:
- Students using and despite the rule.

[Stage: We Do | Combining]
66:
SAY:
- 'New challenge. Join these sentences using one of: for, nor, but, yet.'
- 'Storm Boy did not hesitate. Storm Boy did not wait for someone else to act.'
- 'Whiteboards. Three minutes.'

DO:
- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'Storm Boy did not hesitate, nor did he wait for someone else to act.'
- Note that nor flips the verb order ('did he' not 'he did').

ENABLING & EXTENDING:
ENABLING PROMPT:
- Task: discuss with a partner before writing - which FANBOYS word matches the meaning?
- Extra Notes: nor pairs with negative ideas. Both ideas here are negatives.
EXTENDING PROMPT:
- Task: rewrite using 'and'. Compare which sounds stronger.

WATCH FOR:
- Students who pick or; remind them or shows a choice.

[Stage: Extension | Combining]
67:
SAY:
- 'Read this sentence chorally with me.'
- 'There was a great gust of wind that lifted Mr Percival sideways, and he dropped the line across the drowning ship.'
- 'Identify the pronoun reference and the coordinating conjunction.'
- 'Whiteboards: pronoun first, then FANBOYS word. Three, two, one, show.'

DO:
- Scan. Pronoun: he. FANBOYS: and.
- Ask: 'Why is and the right FANBOYS word here?'

CFU CHECKPOINT:
Technique: Whiteboard Show
Script:
- 'Hold up your pronoun and your FANBOYS word.'
- Scan for: 80% identify he and and.
PROCEED:
- Move to the booklet task.
PIVOT:
- Most likely misconception: students point to 'his' or 'across' as the join.
- Reteach by re-marking on the board: circle the comma, the FANBOYS word and the pronoun.
- Re-check: 'Show me the FANBOYS word - it goes after the comma.'

WATCH FOR:
- Students who copy the whole sentence rather than naming the two parts.

[Stage: We Do | Combining]

- Circulate.
- Reveal: 'There was a great gust of wind that lifted and flung Mr Percival sideways. Mr Percival dropped the line across the drowning ship.'

[Stage: We Do | Build Two]

- 'Replace with he. Pick a FANBOYS word - and works for two events together.'
- 'Add a comma. Three minutes.'

- Reveal: 'There was a great gust of wind that lifted and flung Mr Percival sideways, and he dropped the line across the drowning ship.'
